text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- Some 60 percent of Austrians say political extremism, particularly from the far right, is on the increase, but only 36 percent see a potential danger to society, a new poll shows.
- Several shops in Austria's biggest shopping center SCS opened on Sunday amid strong protest from labour unions.
- Textile employers' head Peter Pfneisl says employees should not go another year without a pay increase. DIE PRESSE

- Social Affairs Minister Lore Hostasch said the outcome of a study currently under way would decide whether she will initiate a reform of Austria's pension system. Experts say the system will break down by the year 2030 unless it is overhauled.

- Former foreign minister Alois Mock told the newspaper in an interview the Iranian government had threatened the Austrian government repeatedly not to prosecute the alleged murderers of three Kurdish leaders in 1989.
- Tough import restrictions imposed by the Czech Republic are hurting Austrian exporters.

- Mobilkom, the mobile phone subsidiary of the Austrian telecoms and postal monopoly, on Tuesday will decide on its new strategic partner. Tele Danmark and Italy's Stet are said to be competing for a minority stake in the company.
- The outlook for the Vienna bourse remains positive after shares gained some two percent over the past week.
- Bank Austria said a report by investment bank Goldman Sachs, which put the value of the City of Vienna's liability guarantee for the bank at some 250 million schillings, was only a draft.
- Ski jumper Andreas Goldberger admitted to having used cocaine once at a Vienna disco.
- A European Union (EU) commission of experts will study Austrian border controls to evaluate whether the country is fit to join the EU's Schengen agreement in October.
- Telecoms and postal monopoly PTA plans to take a 25 percent stake in postal savings bank PSK.
